body_markdown:
There’s a scene that replays in my head often, one I can’t quite let slip by. It’s from late September 2024. I was lying on my side, welding, in the back of my 1976 International Scout Traveler, in my father’s barn.


The air was cool but tinged by late summer humidity and mixed with the crispness of the oncoming fall. A small Bluetooth speaker lay next to my shoulder, cocooning me in the dulcet tones of Patsy Cline’s “Walkin’ After Midnight,” which made tinny echos off the sheet metal around me. Ms. Cline’s soporific voice was interrupted occasionally by the buzzing, crackling snaps of my welder, as I joined sheet metal floorboards to the Traveler’s corroded orange tub.


Nick Jaynes


Nick Jaynes


If, 12 months prior, you had described this scene to me, I simply wouldn’t have believed you. All of it was so far from my reality at the time. Yet there I was, rebuilding—albeit haphazardly—a vintage 4×4 in my father’s barn—a man with whom I’ve forever had a strained relationship.


I love reliving that moment. It’s my happy place. When I am anxious or stressed, I go there. My heart slows and my blood pressure drops.


All because of a project I unintentionally undertook, without envisioning how it would become a turning point in my life. Over the course of 13 months, I would gain new skills, a greater sense of self-reliance, and a renewed relationship with my father.


If you’re looking for tips and tricks on how to take on your first vehicle refurbishment, this isn’t that story; you’ll want to check out Jim Pickering’s[Project Cheap Camaro](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/project-cheap-camaro-an-introduction/) for that.


## The Barn


Nick Jaynes


I wrote about the[arc of my Traveler rebuild in April](https://www.hagerty.com/media/driving/the-suffering-is-the-point-on-the-trail-in-a-scout-with-needs/) , so I won’t rehash it here. But it was kicked off by cavalierly buying the Traveler sight unseen, only later to discover its bodywork was run through with rust. Existential dread set in at first, fearing I’d thrown away[$13,000 on a scrapper](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/international_(ihc)/scout_traveler/1976/1976-international_(ihc)-scout_traveler-base?id=aCn1I000000D63aSAC) . After a week of processing my position, I determined to go all-in on the Traveler—to cut out the bad metal and replace it with new.


“This is the summer I learn to weld,” I proclaimed aloud to myself as I stared at the orange hulk. I started light disassembly of the Traveler in the incredibly steep driveway of my suburban home but quickly realized it was not an ideal spot for such an undertaking. I needed a bit more room. I recalled the modest, unused barn on my father’s property 15 minutes away.


Built by his late wife and her then-husband in the early 1990s, the barn sat catty-corner to the main house and was essentially an unfinished, uninsulated 1.5-car garage used to store a 16-foot speed boat. After my dad moved into the home in the early aughts, the boat was sold and the barn became a repository for yard equipment, including a small riding mower. Having given up mowing his own property years ago, he sold the mower and the barn remained mostly empty, save a few rusting spades and hoes—artifacts from my stepmother’s gardening endeavors.


I called my dad, who was newly widowed, and asked if I could—as a birthday gift—use the barn for the Traveler. He agreed. Moving the truck and some tools into the barn came with a cost greater than simply cashing in an early birthday present, however. It also meant that I’d be vulnerable to pop-ins by my father. Without a better place for the Traveler, though, I fired it up and drove it out there.


## Welding


Nick Jaynes


Nick Jaynes


With the Traveler safely under the eaves of the barn, my first assignment was to get the bad metal out, so new could go in. I spent most of June and July using a proper mix of tools to get the rusty bits out—reciprocating saw, angle grinder, bolt cutters, shears, hacksaw, and a pry bar.


I ordered re-popped sheet metal components from a few International Scout parts houses. While I waited for them to arrive, I turned to welding—something I’d never done before. I bought a Harbor Freight welder on sale for the 4th of July. And I paid my friend Willy, a professional metal fabricator, for an hour of his time to show me the ropes.


I practiced on a few bits of scrap metal I’d picked up at the steel yard, quickly got bored, then turned to patching holes in the passenger rocker panel—tack welds at first, then going whole hog and laying down some beads. I felt such an immense sense of accomplishment from simply filling a roughly four- by five-inch hole I’d cut in the rocker.


Raised by erudite indoorsy yuppies, I found welding as foreign as Mandarin Chinese or the plotlines of WWE. My mother’s version of roughing it is showing up to the hotel without a reservation.


Since I was a child, if I couldn’t figure something out on my own or it didn’t sink in on the first pass from a teacher, I’d freeze up. I’d feel paralyzed with anxiety. This led to more than three decades of my asking for help, letting the helper do it, and moving on without internalizing the lesson. I’d describe myself then as a capable-incapable man.


Welding on the Traveler flipped that script: There was no one to do it for me. I had to learn. I had to get it done. That was that.


## Pop-ins


Nick Jaynes


As expected, my dad popped down regularly for visits. Now alone in a large home on acreage, with few friends or hobbies, he found in me a prime source of social interaction.


“How manly!” he’d proclaim, standing there in decades-old Sperry Topsiders and a pullover fleece as I welded on the Traveler.


We’ve always had a fraught relationship, my father and me. A British-born doctor, he hoped my mother would birth his clone. I was anything but. To his chagrin, in fact, I was everything he was not—naturally athletic, quick-witted, and gregarious. Crucially, and this was my original sin, I was not scientific or mathematical whatsoever. “The doctor,” as I call him, loved numbers. Math made my brain go numb. He soured on me early, convinced I was defective, and proclaimed to my mother that I’d never reach his level of success.


When the doctor would pop down to the barn for a visit, I’d have to pause the task at hand and summarily greet him and listen to his stories of rejoining the dating pool for the first time in a quarter century.


Over the weeks, however, my dad softened a bit and began letting down his guard. He started asking me for my advice about dating and living alone. *How does one find meaning? How do you stave off loneliness? What does it even look like to love yourself?* In between beads of welds, the doctor and I got into some pretty existential topics. The energy in the barn began to shift.


Nick Jaynes


I started to see him not as a disapproving overlord but as the flawed, increasingly frail man he was, floundering through loneliness and self-acceptance accented by fits of insecurity and co-dependence. He grew to see me, I like to think, as less of a broken child and more of a self-driven adult with skills disparate from his own—but valuable ones, nonetheless. He even asked me for my advice from time to time—I don’t think he ever heeded it. The fact he asked, though, spoke volumes.


The Traveler project was something he could never and would never take on himself. He doesn’t know or care about cars. He sees having a car that is more than a transportation appliance as deeply frivolous. Despite this, he became invested in my Traveler project. Any time he heard a loud engine roar to life (usually my Godzilla-powered Super Duty), he’d rush down to see if the Traveler was being fired up for the first time since the refurbishment began.


## Reward


Trevor Ryan


When I recount the Traveler project to folks, I tell them it was the most rewarding experience of my life. My ego was damaged from buying a truck for $13,000 that should have been scrapped. However, I was able to pivot, learn new skills, and grow my confidence. There are a half dozen or so vignettes, like the evening of welding while Patsy Cline serenaded me, that remain with me.


In addition to giving me a great sense of accomplishment, the Traveler also brought my dad and me closer. We’re not best friends. We still don’t really “get” one another. But we speak and see each other more often than we ever have. We rebuilt our relationship 20 minutes at a time over the span of a year, in between welds.


I don’t want to tell you that every car refurbishment will be so meaningful. Chances are it won’t. But my hastiness and car-purchasing bravado unwittingly led me to a lesson I really needed to learn—about myself and my father.


The other day, a guy in his 20s was over at the barn to buy some used wheels and tires from me. He spotted the Traveler and asked about it. I gave him the elevator pitch on my rebuild, a “frame-on frame-off” I like to call it, since 90% of the floors were removed while leaving the tub and front clip bolted to the frame rails.


“How’d you know how to do that?” the guy asked.


“I didn’t,” I chuckled. “That’s the only way to learn, by just doing it. You’ll be surprised what you pick up along the way.”
